slides.title: Chapter 2: How Bitcoin Works
slides.notes: Chapter 1 asked what Bitcoin is. Chapter 2 follows one payment, Alice paying Bob's Store, from the invoice to the blockchain. Every number in this deck was computed with the chapter's own Python library.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.take: Six parts, three true stories, fourteen examples
slides.notes: The route has six parts that follow one payment from the invoice to the spending. Three true stories and fourteen code examples are spread across them, and every example has a picture of its result.

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers

items: What do Alice's payment and Bob's invoice contain?
Why must inputs equal outputs plus a fee, and where does change come from?
How does a wallet choose coins and build the outputs?
How does a payment travel to a miner and into a block?
What makes a payment harder to reverse with each confirmation?
Which rules does every node check, and what if a block breaks one?

slides.notes: The six questions are the chapter's own, rewritten so that each has an answer on a slide. We return to them in the summary. A reader who can answer all six has understood the chapter.

slides.title: The chapter in one picture
slides.take: Six steps, one payment: from invoice to a spendable coin
slides.notes: Six steps carry one payment. Alice reads an invoice, a transaction is formed, coins are chosen, the wallet builds and signs it, a miner puts it in a block, and Bob can spend it. The parts of this deck follow the same path.

slides.title: Buying from an Online Store
slides.sub: Alice pays Bob's Store: one real payment, followed all the way

items.meaning: One payment is followed from the shop's invoice to the blockchain.
items.analogy: Think of tracking a parcel from the shop to your door.

items.meaning: Users, wallets, nodes and miners share one record that nobody owns.
items.analogy: Think of a town where every shop keeps an identical ledger.

items.meaning: The smallest unit: one hundred-millionth of a bitcoin.
items.analogy: Think of the cent, only a million times smaller.

slides.notes: Part 1 starts where Alice does: with an invoice from an online store. We meet the whole system first, then the smallest unit of money and the link that carries the invoice.

slides.title: Four roles, one network
slides.take: No single owner: wallets sign, nodes check, miners bundle
slides.notes: Four roles share the work. Users hold wallets that sign payments, nodes check the rules and pass transactions on, and miners bundle waiting transactions into blocks that everyone copies. Nobody owns the record.

slides.title: Five free bitcoins for every visitor
slides.sub: 11 June 2010 · how a first coin reached its owner

items.cap: Picture: Gavin Andresen, Web Summit 2014 - Stephen McCarthy, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHO Gavin Andresen, a software developer who later led the Bitcoin software after Satoshi Nakamoto left.
WHAT A website that gave five bitcoins to every visitor who solved a CAPTCHA.
WHERE A website announced on the bitcointalk forum; Andresen worked from Massachusetts.
WHY Almost nowhere sold bitcoin in 2010, so he gave coins away to seed the first users.
HOW He stocked the site with 1,100 of his own bitcoins and paid five to each request.

items.who: Gavin Andresen, the developer Satoshi later handed the project to
items.where: freebitcoins.appspot.com, announced on the bitcointalk forum

slides.take: Before exchanges, distribution itself had to be invented
slides.notes: Alice needs bitcoin before she can pay Bob. In 2010 there was almost nowhere to buy it, so Gavin Andresen gave five coins to every visitor of his website. Thousands of people got their first bitcoin this way.

slides.title: Satoshis are whole numbers
slides.sub: Converting the invoice amount without decimals
slides.take: Inside the network every amount is a whole number of satoshis
slides.notes: Bitcoin counts in satoshis, one hundred-millionth of a bitcoin. Decimals are only for people. Converting with whole numbers keeps every digit, which floating point would not.

slides.title: Reading Bob's invoice
slides.sub: A payment link is a small, readable address
slides.take: One link carries the address, the amount and the label
slides.notes: BIP 21 defines the bitcoin link that wallets and QR codes use. We split it into its parts with the standard library. The wallet then knows whom to pay, how much, and what to call the payee.

slides.title: Bitcoin Transactions
slides.sub: Inputs, outputs, chains and change

items.meaning: Inputs spend earlier outputs; outputs lock new amounts to new owners.
items.analogy: Think of handing over banknotes and receiving new ones.

items.meaning: Each input points to an earlier output, back to where the coins began.
items.analogy: Think of a trail of signed receipts, each naming the one before.

items.meaning: Part of a spent coin returns to you as a new output.
items.analogy: Think of paying with a 20 note for a 15 item and getting 5 back.

slides.notes: Part 2 opens the payment itself. A transaction is a ledger entry: it spends earlier outputs and creates new ones, and the difference is the fee.

slides.title: Inputs and outputs
slides.take: An input spends an earlier output; an output creates a new one
slides.notes: A transaction is double-entry bookkeeping: the inputs on the left, the outputs on the right, and the difference is the fee. An input spends an earlier output; an output locks an amount to a new owner.

slides.title: Inputs equal outputs plus the fee
slides.sub: Alice's payment as double-entry bookkeeping
slides.take: Whatever the outputs do not claim becomes the miner's fee
slides.notes: A transaction balances like a ledger. The inputs add up to 100,000 satoshis and the outputs to 95,000. The difference of 5,000 is written nowhere; it is implied, and the miner collects it.

slides.title: The txid is shown backwards
slides.sub: The same 32 bytes in two orders
slides.take: Explorers show the identifier in reverse byte order
slides.notes: The identifier of Alice's earlier transaction is a 32-byte hash. Inside a transaction it is stored one way, and block explorers print it the other way round. Reversing the bytes converts between them.

slides.title: Size in virtual bytes and the fee rate
slides.sub: How a miner compares transactions
slides.take: Miners rank transactions by fee per virtual byte
slides.notes: Alice's transaction weighs 569 units, which is 143 virtual bytes. Her fee of 5,000 satoshis divided by 143 gives about 35 satoshis per virtual byte. Blocks have limited room, so miners pick the best rates first.

slides.title: A chain of transactions
slides.take: Follow the arrows backwards to find where a coin came from
slides.notes: Figure 2-3 shows three linked transactions. Each input names an earlier output, so the coins can be traced back; an output that nobody has spent yet is a coin that still exists.

slides.title: Which outputs are still unspent
slides.sub: Walking the chain of figure 2-3
slides.take: Unspent outputs are the coins that exist right now
slides.notes: Each transaction in the chain spends an earlier output and creates new ones. Collecting what was spent leaves the unspent outputs. Wallets and nodes keep exactly this set, because only these coins can be spent.

slides.title: Coin Selection
slides.sub: Which coins to spend, and what shape the payment takes

items.meaning: Payment, consolidation and batching are shapes of inputs and outputs.
items.analogy: Think of a single cheque, a deposit of coins and a payroll run.

items.meaning: Many small inputs are merged into one output.
items.analogy: Think of swapping a jar of small coins for one banknote.

items.meaning: A fresh address of your own that receives the change.
items.analogy: Think of a new envelope addressed to yourself.

slides.notes: Part 3 asks how a wallet chooses what to spend. Coins are spent whole, so the choice decides the change, and the same rule produces payments, consolidations and batches.

slides.title: Coin selection: pick, pay, change back
slides.sub: A wallet chooses coins to cover a payment
slides.take: Coins are taken whole, so the surplus returns as change
slides.notes: A wallet cannot cut a coin in two. It takes whole coins until the payment is covered, then sends the surplus back to itself as change. Real wallets use smarter rules, but this is the idea.

slides.title: Three common shapes of a transaction
slides.sub: Counting inputs, outputs and the fee
slides.take: The same ledger rule fits every shape
slides.notes: Three forms cover most transactions. A payment spends a coin and returns change. A consolidation merges many small coins into one, and batching pays many people at once. In every case inputs minus outputs is the fee.

slides.title: Constructing a Transaction
slides.sub: The wallet assembles, prices and signs the payment

items.meaning: Find unspent outputs that together cover the payment and the fee.
items.analogy: Think of counting coins onto the counter before paying.

items.meaning: Write down who receives how much, and where the change goes.
items.analogy: Think of filling in the payee and the amount on a cheque.

items.meaning: Inputs minus outputs: the difference that the miner keeps.
items.analogy: Think of the postage stamp that pays the post office.

slides.notes: Part 4 builds Alice's transaction step by step. The wallet finds inputs, writes the outputs, leaves a fee and signs, and the fee rate decides how much change comes back.

slides.title: From coins to a signed transaction
slides.take: The wallet only decides inputs, outputs and fee; the rules do the rest
slides.notes: The wallet builds Alice's transaction in five steps. It finds the inputs, writes the outputs, leaves the fee, signs every input and broadcasts the result to a node, which passes it on.

slides.title: A higher fee rate leaves less change
slides.sub: Pricing the payment before signing
slides.take: The wallet decides the fee; the change is what remains
slides.notes: When the wallet builds the outputs it chooses a fee rate. The fee is the rate times the size. The change output is what is left after paying Bob and the fee, so a higher rate means smaller change.

slides.title: Adding the Transaction to the Blockchain
slides.sub: From a node's inbox to a block that others build on

items.meaning: Miners search for a number that makes a block of transactions valid.
items.analogy: Think of rolling dice until a very rare number turns up.

items.meaning: Every block built on top makes the payment harder to reverse.
items.analogy: Think of more witnesses signing a contract.

items.meaning: The first block of the chain, fixed in the software of every node.
items.analogy: Think of page one of a ledger, printed into the binding.

slides.notes: Part 5 follows the signed transaction to a block. Miners search for a lucky number, the block is added, and every block on top makes the payment harder to reverse.

slides.title: Height, depth and confirmations
slides.take: More blocks on top means a payment that is harder to reverse
slides.notes: Alice's transaction sits in block 277,316. A block's height counts from the genesis block, and its depth counts the blocks on top. Each block on top is one more confirmation, and a block explorer shows all of it.

slides.title: One more zero, many more tries
slides.sub: Mining as a search for a lucky number
slides.take: Mining is a search; more zeros means more work
slides.notes: A miner changes a number, the nonce, and hashes again until the result starts with enough zeros. Nobody can shortcut the search, but anyone can check the answer with one hash. The network sets how many zeros are needed.

slides.title: The first block header is 80 bytes
slides.sub: Hashing the genesis block's header
slides.take: A block's name is the hash of its 80-byte header
slides.notes: The genesis block was mined on 3 January 2009. Its header packs a version, the previous block, a summary of the transactions, a time, a difficulty and a nonce. Hashing it twice gives the famous name that starts with ten zeros.

slides.title: Nine pages, one table of probabilities
slides.sub: 31 October 2008 · section 11 of the white paper

items.cap: Picture: Satoshi bust, Budapest - Fekist, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHO Satoshi Nakamoto, the pseudonymous author, writing to a cryptography mailing list.
WHAT A nine-page paper whose section 11 tabulates an attacker's chance of catching up.
WHERE The metzdowd.com cryptography mailing list; the PDF now sits on bitcoin.org.
WHY To show with numbers that waiting for confirmations makes a double spend unlikely.
HOW A random walk models the race of an honest chain against a secret one; the next slide reruns it.

items.who: Satoshi Nakamoto, the pseudonymous author, writing to the readers of the metzdowd.com cryptography mailing list
items.where: the metzdowd.com cryptography mailing list and bitcoin.org

slides.take: A confirmation is a probability statement, and you can compute it
slides.notes: The white paper reached its readers on 31 October 2008. Its section 11 does something rare for a systems paper: it computes the attacker's odds. The next slide reruns that computation.

slides.title: Nakamoto's catch-up table, recomputed
slides.sub: Section 11 of the white paper, run again
slides.take: Every confirmation makes a reversal much less likely
slides.notes: Section 11 of the white paper computes how likely an attacker is to catch up. We reran the formula and obtained the paper's table to seven places. The chance drops fast with every block, which is why six confirmations became a habit.

slides.title: Spending the Transaction
slides.sub: When Bob may spend, and what every node checks first

items.meaning: Rules that every node checks the same way; a block that breaks one is refused.
items.analogy: Think of the rules of chess that every player and referee enforce.

items.meaning: A website where anyone can look up blocks, transactions and addresses.
items.analogy: Think of a parcel tracker for money.

slides.notes: Part 6 closes the loop. Bob can spend his new output, and every node checks the same rules, so that a block which breaks one is refused.

slides.title: The reward halves every 210,000 blocks
slides.sub: One of the consensus rules, in one line
slides.take: Halving is a rule every node enforces, not a promise
slides.notes: The block reward is a consensus rule. Every node computes it the same way and refuses a block that claims more. Halving every 210,000 blocks, about four years, is what limits the total number of bitcoin.

slides.title: The day someone printed 184 billion bitcoin
slides.sub: 15 August 2010 · block 74,638

items.cap: Picture: Bitcoin logo - Grayliptrot, public domain, Wikimedia Commons - a stand-in, since no free picture of the event exists

items: WHO An unknown attacker; Jeff Garzik, who spotted the block; Satoshi Nakamoto, who patched the software.
WHAT A block paid out about 184 billion bitcoin, thousands of times the 21 million limit.
WHERE Block 74,638 of the Bitcoin chain, discussed live on the bitcointalk forum.
WHY Two outputs were so large that their sum overflowed and passed the checks; no rule limited the amounts.
HOW Garzik flagged the block within the hour; Satoshi shipped version 0.3.10 about five hours later and the honest chain overtook it.

items.who: Jeff Garzik, the developer who spotted the block, and Satoshi Nakamoto, who patched the software; the attacker is unknown
items.where: block 74,638, discussed live on the bitcointalk forum

slides.take: Validation by every node is the immune system - and it worked
slides.notes: On 15 August 2010 block 74,638 created about 184 billion bitcoin out of an overflow. Every node checks every rule, and this one rule was missing. Within hours the software was fixed and the honest chain, without the forged coins, won.

slides.title: Two outputs that wrapped around
slides.sub: Block 74,638 and the value overflow of 2010
slides.take: One overflow created 184 billion bitcoin; one new rule ended it
slides.notes: In August 2010 a block paid out two huge outputs. Their sum overflowed a 64-bit integer, so the software thought the outputs were small. A new rule was shipped within hours, and the honest chain, without the forged coins, won.

slides.take: Inputs, outputs, fee, mining, confirmations, rules
slides.notes: Each row answers one of the six opening questions in a line. If you can say each answer in your own words, using the everyday pictures of this chapter, you have the chapter.
